activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
story:
The camp bus smelled like sunscreen and granola bars, and Carson had already memorized the back of the driver's head by the time they were ten minutes down the highway. He was going away to camp for the very first time, three whole weeks, and everything felt like the start of an adventure. His cabin duffel sat under his knees like a loyal dog.

"We're going to the lake on day one," said Ilya, who was in the seat beside him and had been to this camp twice before. "Afternoon swim, then a whole afternoon on the sand. Last year a kid in my cabin got fried like a lobster."

"But he wore sunscreen," Carson said. He had watched the kid's older brother, Molly's brother actually, describe it at the bus stop. "He put it on in the morning. Everyone saw him put it on."

Ilya shrugged and started unwrapping a granola bar.

Carson couldn't stop thinking about it. A kid who wore sunscreen got burned anyway, and a kid who wore none got burned too. That didn't seem like sunscreen didn't work. It seemed like something hidden was going on, some pattern he couldn't see directly. He decided to run a test, the way scientists in books did. He would put sunscreen on in the morning like everyone else, and he would watch his own arms like a hawk all day.

At the lake, Carson slathered on sunscreen at nine in the morning, right after the flagpole. He swam. He dried off. He built a sand fort with Molly, hauling wet bucket after wet bucket, sweating in the sun. Around noon he checked his forearms in the luminous glare off the water. Faint pink, like a slow warning.

"Your arm looks like a hot dog," said Molly, which did not illustrate anything helpful.

Then it clicked. The boy from last year had put sunscreen on once, in the morning, and stayed outside all afternoon. A whole afternoon. If sunscreen wore off and washed off, one morning application couldn't possibly last. Carson rummaged in his duffel, found the bottle, and put it on again. Then again after his afternoon swim, and once more after the sweaty fort building, counting on his fingers: morning, midday, after swimming. About every two hours, like a schedule, like a little algorithm you could follow without thinking.

By dinnertime his arms were only faintly warm, not burned. Ilya, who had done one morning application and nothing else, was glowing like a stop sign and groaning every time his shirt touched his shoulders.

"You have to reapply," Carson said, holding up the bottle. "Every two hours, and right after swimming or sweating. That's the whole trick."

Ilya stared at him. "That's it? That's the whole secret?"

"That's the whole secret," said Carson, and tossed him the bottle.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Salt melts ice by lowering the temperature at which water freezes, but ordinary rock salt stops working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius (14 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
The snow day arrived like a surprise party, and Avery found the invitation taped to her shoe: a note from her dad on the kitchen table. "Shovel the steps, then go be a snowman. Signed, Management." She pulled on her boots, grabbed the shovel, and stopped at the second step. Dad had salted it yesterday, but the ice lay there fat and shiny and completely unfazed, like a cat ignoring its own name.

Avery checked the thermometer nailed to the porch rail. It read two degrees Fahrenheit, which was so cold her breath made little clouds that seemed reluctant to leave. She scattered more salt and watched. Nothing. A nasty thought began to draft its way through her mind, cold as the wind: maybe the salt wasn't broken; maybe the cold was. Yesterday it had been warm enough that the salt had chewed the ice into gray slush. Today the same salt sat on top like sprinkles on a frozen cake. She touched the ice with her bare finger for exactly one second, then spent ten seconds recovering. Solid as a countertop.

At the sledding hill, Graydon and Brian were arguing about whose run was fastest. "You're just heavier," Graydon said. "It's science." Avery held up her phone, which showed the weather app and the number fourteen. "Fourteen degrees Fahrenheit is the magic line. Below that, rock salt just quits. Yesterday was twenty-nine and the salt worked. Today we're way under, and it doesn't." Brian squinted at her. "You tested this?" "I did an experiment on my steps. The results were icy."

They built a jump at the bottom of the hill instead, an intricate wall of packed snow with a lip like a spoon. Avery went first, screaming the whole way, and landed in a puff of white. From inside the drift, her voice came up muffled: "Graydon! Your formula is wrong! I went fastest and I weigh the least!" Graydon peered down at her. "New rule," he announced. "Snowmen get disqualified."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of demand says that when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it, and when the price falls they buy more, as long as nothing else changes.
story:
The line for the Aster June tickets wrapped twice around the block, and Addison had been standing in it long enough to know every crack in the sidewalk. It smelled like hot pretzels and rain that hadn't fallen yet. Ahead of her, a man in a yellow cap held up two tickets and shouted, "Two hundred each, folks, two hundred." Behind him, the box office sign read forty dollars. Almost nobody stepped out of line to buy his. Addison counted: eleven people walked past him without even slowing down.

A text buzzed in her pocket. It was Charly: "My brother says scalpers lower the price right before doors open if they still have tickets. He watched it happen last summer. Also bring sunscreen, you sound burnt already." Addison wrote back, "Not burnt, just orange. Tell your brother he's a genius." She looked at Yellow Cap again. He had lowered nothing so far, and his stack of tickets looked meticulous, fanned out like a card trick, every edge aligned. She decided to test Charly's brother's theory with her own eyes, because trusting a rumor felt like something her grandmother would do with a chain email.

She also had a backup plan. The lemonade cart near the corner had been doing brisk business at two dollars a cup, and the queue for it was almost as long as the one for tickets. Then the vendor called out, "Four dollars now, last of the batch!" and the line for lemonade evaporated like puddle water in July. Two girls who had been waiting walked away without cups. Only one man bought one, and he looked unhappy about it. Addison filed that away. When the price went up, people bought less. She guessed the opposite was true too, though she hadn't seen it yet.

Doors opened in twenty minutes when Yellow Cap finally cracked. "A hundred fifty," he called. Two people peeled off from the far end of the line, but he still had a thick stack. "A hundred," he tried, quieter. Five more came over, and suddenly he was selling fast, hands grabbing, bills flying, his neat fan of tickets collapsing into a scramble. The lower the price went, the more people bought. Addison watched the whole thing happen like a slow door swinging open in her head.

She got to the box office window just as the cashier shook her head. "Sold out." Addison stood there for a second, feeling the loss settle in. Then she heard Charly's voice from somewhere behind, breathless and triumphant: "I got two! Face value! A guy in a yellow cap panicked and sold them to me for forty." Addison turned around. "Forty?" "Forty. My brother calls it the law of demand, by the way." Addison took the ticket Charly held out, warm from her friend's hand, and said, "Best economics lesson I ever stood in line for. Now get us a lemonade, it's two dollars again."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and pretzels, and Hudson had been regretting his seat choice since the parking lot. He'd picked the row behind Anaelle, who hadn't stopped talking about the physics hall, when he really wanted to sit with Evelynn, who had promised to show him the trick with the prism that could refract sunlight into a rainbow across the whole cafeteria table. That had been two weeks ago. He could still have switched seats. He hadn't, and now the class was funneling through the science center's glass doors.

Ms. Wardak handed out maps. "Half the day is the light and optics floor," she said, "and half is the heritage wing, where they keep the old fire engine. Stay with your group."

Anaelle grabbed Hudson's sleeve. "Optics first. I've been planning a siege on that laser maze since September. I'm going to beat the record this time."

The heritage wing turned out to be quieter than the optics floor, all dark wood and brass. The fire engine sat in the middle like a sleeping animal, and beside it hung a painting of a white dog covered in black spots, standing proudly beside a team of horses. Evelynn stopped in front of it and frowned. "Why would a fire station hang up a spotted dog?"

Nobody answered. The guide was across the room. Hudson stared at the dog, then at the engine, then back at the horses in the painting. The engine was old, the kind pulled by horses, not driven by a motor. A dog that ran with horses. A dog that could clear the street ahead.

"Maybe the dog went first," he said slowly. "Running ahead of the carriage, barking people out of the way. Look at the painting again. The dog's out in front of the horses, like it's leading." He thought of his own dog at home, who herded everyone toward the food bowl at dinner time without ever being taught.

Evelynn pulled out the little pamphlet from the rack by the door and flipped through it. "It says Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of the horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way." She looked up. "You basically got it."

"The whole thing?" Anaelle asked, appearing behind them, out of breath from the laser maze, where the siege had apparently failed. "Ugh. Fine. That's almost as good as a record."

"There's a picture of one in the optics hall," she added, deflating slightly. "It's in the shadow exhibit. If you come now, I'll show you." Hudson thought about the prism he'd missed on the bus, the seat he could have chosen and didn't.

"Lead the way," he said, and this time he followed.

In the dark of the shadow exhibit, a glass case held a small porcelain Dalmatian beside a model carriage. Light passed through the case's curved lid and refracted, throwing wobbling spots of brightness across the ceiling, more spots than any dog could ever own. Anaelle tilted her head back and laughed.

"That," she said, "is worth losing for."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
story:
The bacon was Wyatt's job this morning, and he took it seriously. Dad had gone down to the lake to fill the water jugs, Harris was still snoring in the other tent, and Wyatt had the camp stove and a heavy pan all to himself. He laid the strips in carefully, the way Dad had shown him last summer, and watched the edges turn from pink to crisp. In the doorway of the tent, Harris finally stirred and emerged with his hair sticking straight up.

"You burn it and I'm not eating it," Harris said, sitting on the cooler. "I need a good breakfast. Today I'm finally going to beat Eric in the fire-building contest, and I can't do that on an empty stomach."

"It won't burn," Wyatt said. "Probably." He reached for the salt to elaborate on his plan: eggs after the bacon, then toast on the griddle, a whole breakfast with his own name on it. That was when the pan caught. A flare of orange licked up from the grease, then another, and flames stood a foot above the stove.

Harris scrambled backward, knocking over the water jug. "Put water on it!" he yelled, grabbing the jug and starting to unscrew the cap. Water was sloshing toward the pan in his hands.

"Stop!" Wyatt's arm shot out. He remembered last summer, standing at this same stove while the grease flared, and Dad not reaching for the water jug at all. Dad had reached for the lid instead. Wyatt turned the burner off and slid the lid over the pan, cutting off the fire like a door closing. The flames vanished under the metal. The pan sat there, dark and quiet, a thin thread of vapor curling out from under the rim.

Harris stared, the jug still in his hands. "How did you know that?"

"Never pour water on a grease fire," Wyatt said, taking the jug from him and setting it down. "It turns to steam instantly and throws the burning oil everywhere. Turn off the heat and put a lid on it instead. That smothers it. My dad did it right here last year." He lifted the lid a crack, peered in, and closed it again. "Give it a minute."

Harris exhaled slowly. "I almost made it a hundred times worse." He looked at Wyatt with something like new respect. "Okay. New deal. You teach me the pan stuff, and I'll teach you fire-building, and between us we'll beat Eric at something."

Wyatt lifted the lid again. The bacon underneath was dark at the edges but saved, and the pan was cool enough to touch. He slid the strips onto a plate and cracked two eggs into the leftover grease, which shimmered, calm and golden, in the morning light. "First lesson," he said, tapping the spatula on the pan's rim. "Pay attention, Harris. This one's important."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move.
story:
Rain hammered the classroom windows like a monsoon had wandered off course and found the chess club instead. Rose sat across from Julie, who had already lost twice and was sliding her bishop in slow circles, stalling. Lianna leaned over the next desk, watching them the way she watched everything, like she might recruit you for something before the bell.

Rose reached for her knight, lifted it two inches, and felt her whole plan collapse. The square she needed was covered by Julie's rook. She set the knight back down and reached for the pawn instead.

"You have to move it," Julie said, sitting up. "You picked it up."

"No I don't. I put it back."

Lianna appeared beside them like weather. "Touch-move rule. If you deliberately touch one of your own pieces and it has a legal move, you have to move it."

"That's radical," Julie said, delighted.

Rose looked at the board. The knight did have legal moves, just terrible ones, which was worse than having none, somehow. But she had learned something from Lianna besides the rule. She had watched Lianna break up two arguments last week by naming the problem out loud instead of shouting louder. "Okay," Rose said slowly. "The problem isn't whether I touched it. The problem is we never agreed what counts in a friendly game. So here's my offer. We follow touch-move from now on, both of us, every game. But this once, since we never agreed, I take it back and I move the pawn."

Julie drummed her fingers on the table. She wanted the win. Rose could see her doing the math: up a pawn already, and Rose's knight about to wander into a corner for the rest of its life. A win by argument was still a win, but a win on the board was better.

"Deal," Julie said. "Move your pawn. And next game, I'm touching every single one of your pieces before you can."

Lianna wrote something in her notebook and closed it.

"What was that?" Rose asked.

"Nothing. Roster stuff."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting in New Zealand in which two people press their noses and foreheads together, symbolizing the sharing of the breath of life.
story:
Katherine stood at the kitchen counter folding napkins into little fans, because Auntie Pearl had said the party for their New Zealand relatives started at six o'clock sharp, and it was already ten to. Through the opaque curtains she could see headlights sliding up the driveway, one car after another, and her stomach did a small flip. She had never met these cousins before, and she had exactly ten minutes to figure out how to say hello to them without looking silly.

"They're here," called Milo, who lived next door and had been invited because he helped carry the chairs. He pressed his nose against the window so hard it turned white at the tip. "The one in the blue sweater keeps looking at her phone. She looks scared."

That gave Katherine an idea. The girl in the blue sweater was probably her age, probably a new student at her school in September, and probably just as nervous as Katherine was. People who felt nervous, Katherine had noticed, often wanted one good, ordinary thing to happen to them first. At school, Mr. Takahashi always shook hands with new students, and her grandfather hugged everyone, but what if this family did something different? She had seen her aunt press her forehead against a friend's once, at a different party, and she wondered if that was a rule she had never been told. She decided to watch what the aunties did first, before she did anything at all.

The door opened and the smell of roasted lamb and mint rolled out into the September evening. The oldest aunt stepped forward and gently pressed her nose and forehead against the first visitor's nose and forehead, and they stayed like that for a moment, eyes closed, breathing the same air. Katherine watched closely. Then it was her turn, and she copied it exactly, careful not to bump too hard. The girl in the blue sweater, whose name was Madina, blinked at her and whispered, "What was that?"

"It's called a hongi," Madina's mother said, laughing as she set down a gift-wrapped box of chocolates, which Auntie Pearl accepted with both hands and a little bow, the way gifts were given in this house. "We do it in New Zealand. It means we share the breath of life."

Katherine's nervousness seemed to dissolve right there in the hallway. At dinner she noticed Madina waiting, fork hovering, until everyone at the long table had been served before she took a single bite, while Milo, who had already started, froze mid-chew and quietly set his fork down. Down the table, an uncle was explaining to another that the bakery's revenue had doubled since they started selling bread on Saturdays, and Madina leaned toward Katherine and whispered, "Can you teach me the fork thing?" Katherine grinned and slid the bread basket toward her. "Trade you," she whispered back. "You teach me the nose thing again, slower this time."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In rock-paper-scissors, each choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one, so no choice is better than the others.
story:
The fight started over who got the good basketball, the one with real grip instead of the scuffed ball nobody wanted. Kenan said they should settle it with rock-paper-scissors, and then he ruined his own idea by adding, "And I get rock, because rock always wins." Vanessa laughed at him, but Kenan only crossed his arms and stood taller. Hunter could perceive that this was going to end with no game at all, and he wanted the game more than he wanted to be right.

"Prove it," Vanessa said. She threw paper against Kenan's rock and won the round. Kenan grumbled that it was luck, so they played again, and again, right there on the cracked blacktop by the swings. Scissors cut paper. Rock smashed scissors. Paper covered rock. After twenty throws, Hunter kept score on the back of his hand with a pencil stub, and the tally came out nearly even. "It's not luck," Hunter said, showing Kenan the marks. "Each one beats exactly one other and loses to exactly one. Nothing is better." Kenan squinted at the numbers like they might be lying to him.

That night Hunter wrote a note and folded it into a paper airplane, planning to fly it through Kenan's window in the morning, since that was their system for important messages. "Dear Kenan," he wrote, "the ball is versatile, it works for anybody, so the fight is not really about the ball. It is about who decides. Here is my rule: winner of one fair throw picks the ball, loser picks the next game. Your witness in court, Hunter." He knew testimony from a notebook was stronger than yelling, because Kenan respected anything written down.

At the playground the next day, Kenan read the note twice, then held out his fist. "One throw," he said. "Rock against whatever you pick, and the rule is the rule." Hunter shaped his hand into flat paper. "One, two, three." Kenan's rock landed against Hunter's paper, and Vanessa, watching from the monkey bars, called out, "Paper covers rock!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wind makes cold air feel colder because it carries heat away from the skin faster, which is what the wind chill number describes.
story:
The school closing text arrived at 6:58 in the morning, and Noah was already dressed by 7:00. Snow day. He pressed his face against the kitchen window and grinned at the backyard, where the snow lay thick and lush over the picnic table, the swing set, and the dead tomato garden. He was going to build the biggest fort of his life, and he had already nominated the spot: the corner by the fence, where the drifts came up past his boots.

Then he checked the weather app, because his mom made him, and his grin wobbled. It was twenty-one degrees out, which was fine, but below that it said "feels like 9." Nine degrees felt wrong. He shoved the phone in his pocket, found his gloves, and texted Gerald: SNOW DAY GET OVER HERE.

Gerald arrived red-faced and loud, and they started packing blocks. Within ten minutes Noah's fingers ached, and the top of his ear, the stiff part with the cartilage, stung so badly he had to press a mitten against it. "This can't be twenty-one," he said through his scarf. "It was colder than this last week and my hands were fine."

"Twenty-one is what my phone said too," Gerald said. "But it's really windy." He flung a block into the wall and stamped his feet. Noah pulled out his phone again and stared at the two numbers. Twenty-one. Feels like 9. The wind was the only different thing, so he said it out loud. "That lower number is the wind chill. Wind makes cold air feel colder because it carries heat away from your skin faster."

"So the wind is stealing our heat," Gerald said. "Rude."

Noah looked at the fort wall, then at the fence corner, then had the idea. He made Gerald stand in the open yard for thirty seconds, hand bare, then behind the half-built wall, out of the wind, for thirty seconds more. "Behind the wall," Gerald reported, "way warmer. Same snow, same everything." Noah wrote it in the snow with his boot: WALL = WARM. They spent the next hour building the wall higher on the windy side, working faster there, resting in the sheltered corner, checking bare fingers like scientists.

By noon the fort had a roof of branches and a snow chair for each of them, and from inside, out of the wind, it was almost cozy. Gerald poked his head out the doorway, squinted at the bare maple branches bending overhead, and ducked back in. "Wind's picking up," he said. "Hot chocolate emergency. Go."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Signposting words like 'first', 'second' and 'finally' tell listeners where they are in a speech, because they cannot flip back a page the way a reader can.
story:
Anthony's grandfather had agreed to be his practice audience, and for three nights he sat in the kitchen chair narrating back what he remembered of the speech. "You said something about buses, then something about money, then I lost the thread entirely," his grandfather admitted after the third try. "By the middle I couldn't tell if you were on your first point or your last. It was like listening to a ship announce its cargo without a manifest."

Anthony lay awake thinking about that. A reader could flip back a page to check where they were, but a listener couldn't. So the listener needed markers in the air itself, little flags planted in order. He wrote three words at the top of his notecard in sparse, careful letters: first, second, finally. Then he imagined them as glowing buoys floating down a dark river, and his speech as a boat that had to pass each one in turn.

At the tournament on Saturday, the room smelled like chalk and nerves. Saige gave her speech before him, smooth as a stone skipped across a pond, and Beau whispered, "She narrated the whole thing like a tour guide." When Anthony stood up, he pictured the river. "First," he said, and watched the judge write the number one. Somewhere in his mind a buoy lit up green.

Halfway through his second point, a fire truck wailed past the window and half the room turned to look. Anthony's heart banged, but he heard himself say "finally," and the judge's pen moved, and a girl in the front row nodded, finding her place again like someone catching a familiar landmark on a dark road.

Afterward his grandfather found him by the water fountain. "I followed every bit of it this time," he said. "What did you change?"

"Signposting," Anthony said. "Want to hear it again on the drive home?"

His grandfather was already pulling the car keys from his pocket.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: In a round such as 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat', every group sings the same melody but starts at a different time, which creates harmony.
story:
The choir room smelled like wet paint because the school was going to renovate it over the summer, so Mr. Singh had moved practice to the cafeteria, where the acoustics were terrible and the smell of Tuesday's cuisine, soggy pasta, still hung in the air. Noah stood in the second row with Lina and Byron, clutching his folder. In two weeks the choir would sing at the spring concert, and Noah still could not hold his part. Every time the two groups split into harmony, his voice slid over to the melody like a magnet finding its north pole.

"Group two, you're jumping into group one's line again," Mr. Singh said, tapping the piano. "Again from measure twelve."

They tried again. Noah lost it again. He heard the melody, his brain grabbed it, and his own notes vanished. Lina whispered that he wasn't alone, half of group two was drifting, but that didn't make him feel better. He wanted a solo someday, and a boy who couldn't hold a harmony part would never get one.

At lunch, Byron started humming "Row, Row, Row Your Boat," and something clicked in Noah's head. "Wait," he said. "That's a round. Every group sings the same melody, just starting at a different time." Lina frowned, so he stood her and Byron at opposite ends of the table. "Byron, start. Lina, you come in when he reaches 'boat.'" They tried it, giggling, and the two lines wove together into a sound that was neither of them alone. Noah's eyes went wide. The groups weren't singing against each other. They were singing the same song, shifted in time, and the overlap made the harmony. The wrongness he kept hearing was actually the point.

He tested it in practice that afternoon. Instead of fighting the melody group, he listened for how his notes lined up with theirs, like tracking Lina's entrance in the round. When the drift began, he anchored himself to the first group's "boat" and let his own line lean against it. Measure twelve passed. Then twenty. Then the final chord, and his voice was still there, still his.

Mr. Singh lowered his hands and grinned at group two. "Whatever you just did, do it again Thursday."

On the way out, Lina nudged Noah's shoulder. "So was it a real harmony, or just lucky?"

"Harmony," Noah said. "Definitely harmony. Ask me again at the concert."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them.
story:
The four-square court behind the gym had been empty all week because of rain, so when the sun came out on Friday, half of sixth grade migrated there within ten minutes of the lunch bell. Jaxon got a spot in square A right away, which almost never happened. Mara took square B, and Jana and a kid from another class filled C and D.

They played the ordinary way for a while. Then Jaxon hit a line ball, the kind where nobody can say for sure whether it touched the crack or not, and Mara called it out. Jaxon said it was in. Jana put her hand up and said they should just do it over, so they did, and the game went on.

The score crept up. They were playing to eleven, and Jaxon was at nine when Mara served a fast one that he barely got his knuckles on. It wobbled over the net and dropped straight down toward the far corner of her square.

"New rule," Mara said quickly, before the ball even stopped bouncing. "If the ball lands in the corner near the wall, it's a replay. That's the rule."

"You can't make up a rule in the middle of a game," Jaxon said.

"Why not? It's a good rule."

Jaxon thought about it while Jana picked up the ball and held it, waiting. If Mara had said that corner rule at the start, when the score was zero to zero, it would have sounded fine. But she had said it at the exact moment it would save her from losing the point, and probably the game, since he only needed two more.

"Because right now the rule helps you and hurts me," he said. "If we decided it before we started, when we were zero to zero, none of us would know who it would help. That's why rules before a game are fair and rules in the middle of a game aren't."

Mara looked at the corner, then at the scoreboard they had made in art class, a prototype out of cardboard with number cards that slid along a slit. Jaxon had slid his nine into place himself.

"Fine," she said. "Then we make the corner rule official for the next game. But this ball, it was in or out, and we do it over like Jana said."

"Deal," Jaxon said. "And we say it out loud first so it's explicit. Corner near the wall is a replay. Agreed?"

They all agreed, and Jana wrote it on the back of the cardboard scoreboard with a stubby pencil. Then she bounced the serve to Mara, who hit it back clean and hard over the net, and Jaxon lunged for it with both hands.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Showering with soap, especially after exercise, washes away the sweat and bacteria that cause body odor.
story:
The pharmacy smelled like mint and hand lotion, and Isla stood in the deodorant aisle pretending to read shampoo labels. She had skipped her shower after Tuesday's track practice because she was running late, and on Wednesday Xavier had slid his desk two inches away from hers, and Emilie had held her sleeve over her nose during the group project. Nobody said anything. That was the worst part.

The plan had seemed simple: buy deodorant, comply with the new rules of sixth grade, move on. But the shelf held a dozen kinds, solid and gel and spray, and Isla felt a wave of pessimism. What if the problem wasn't something a stick could fix? What if everyone had already decided?

"Isla?" Emilie's voice came from the end of the aisle. She was holding a deodorant too, hiding it behind her binder.

"Doing a science project," Isla said quickly. Both of them knew it was a terrible lie.

Emilie came closer, then stopped, and Isla braced for it. But Emilie's face wasn't disgusted. It was scared. "I switched to morning practices," she said. "And my mom leaves for work at six, and I didn't know you were supposed to shower with soap right after you sweat, because the sweat and the bacteria sit on your skin and that's what makes the smell." She said it all in one breath, like a confession. "Xavier told me. He figured it out because the same thing happened to him last year."

Isla blinked. "Wait. He moved his desk away from me."

"He moved it away from everyone. He thinks he's the smelly one." Emilie held up her deodorant. "Want to go find him at the magazine rack? He's been over there for twenty minutes trying to look casual."

Mr. Brennan waved from behind the counter as they passed. "You two need a basket for those?"

"Not a controversy," Isla said, grinning for the first time in days. "Just a misunderstanding."

Xavier saw them coming and shoved the body spray back on the shelf. Isla held up her own stick where he could see it, and his shoulders dropped an inch, relieved.

"Team shower plan," Emilie announced. "After every practice. Soap, then this."

Xavier grabbed two more from the shelf and dropped them into the basket.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
story:
Ivy had thirty minutes to decide, because the electronics store closed at nine and her mother would drive her there after the library closed. She wanted the ZapPad Pro tablet more than anything, mostly because the ad said everyone at Northfield Middle School already had one.

"You should get it," said Ellia, leaning over her shoulder at the computer. "The ad says it's the most brilliant, thrilling tablet ever made."

"Brilliant and thrilling," said Isra from the next seat. "Those are loaded words. We learned about that. It means the words are chosen to make you feel something instead of think."

"Fine, but look at everything it does." Ivy scrolled the ZapPad page. "It lists five great features. Fast chip, big screen, two cameras, cool colors, and a free game."

Mr. De Vries walked past with a cart of returns. "Library closes in thirty minutes," he said, tapping his watch.

Ivy looked at the five features again. Something bothered her, the way a puzzle bothers you when one piece is missing but you can't see the gap yet. "Ellia, what does your brother's ZapPad run out of fastest?"

"Battery. He charges it like three times a day. He says it's the worst part."

Ivy scrolled the ad from top to bottom. There was no battery life anywhere. Not on the page, not in the video, not in the small print. The video showed a famous singer saying she never left home without it, which Ivy guessed was supposed to count as a reason.

"Five features," Ivy said slowly, "and no battery. That's weird, right? If the battery were good, they'd brag about it."

"So it's probably bad," said Isra.

Ivy searched for reviews and found a testing site. The ZapPad battery lasted four hours. The Comet Max, which cost the same, lasted ten and had a slightly slower chip. The ad only showed the facts that made the ZapPad look good and left out the one that didn't.

"That's called card stacking," Ellia said, reading over her shoulder. "My cousin told me about it. You stack the cards so only your side shows."

"Then the logical move is the Comet Max," Ivy said. "Same price, better battery. And 'everyone has a ZapPad' doesn't even matter. Half our class doesn't." She paused. "What's the singer's motive, though? Why does she care what tablet I buy?"

"She got paid, probably," said Isra.

"Then her opinion contributes nothing," Ivy said. "Ten minutes left."

At eight fifty-two, Ivy wrote the Comet Max on a slip of paper and folded it into her pocket. Mr. De Vries flicked the lights once, the signal to leave. As Ivy pushed through the door into the parking lot, her phone buzzed. It was her mother: "Heading to the store now. Did everyone really get the ZapPad?"

Ivy typed back, "Nope. That was the ad talking. Get the Comet Max, and I'll tell you in the car about the singer who never leaves home without anything."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite.
story:
Marcus woke to a strange silence, the kind that meant snow had obstructed the whole street overnight. The radio confirmed it: no school. His mom had already left for work, and a note on the counter said the landlord was coming to check the furnace, so Marcus should stay outside only until noon.

He did not need to be told twice. Israel knocked on the door before Marcus had finished his cereal, dragging a sled and shouting something about the hill behind Sofie's building. "Come on, it was spontaneous," Israel said, as if Marcus needed convincing. "Nobody planned this. That's the whole point."

The hill was fast and the snow was the dry, squeaky kind that flew up like sugar. They ran up and flew down so many times that Marcus lost count. After a while, though, Israel stopped at the bottom and pulled off one glove. "My fingers are like frozen carrots," he said, wiggling them. "Look, they're white at the tips."

Marcus peeled off his own glove and checked. His fingers were pale too, and when he pressed them together, he could barely feel the pressure. Then he touched his ears and got almost nothing, just a dull thump, like knocking on a wall instead of skin. His toes ached inside his boots, and the tip of his nose had gone from cold to nothing at all. It struck him that these were exactly the parts that acted weird, fingers, toes, ears and nose, while his stomach and legs underneath still felt almost warm.

"So this is the stuff frostbite goes for first," he said. "Not your whole body. Just these." He pulled his hood up, shoved his hands under his arms and looked at Israel. "Let's try one more run and see if keeping these covered changes anything. If my ears still feel dead, we're going in."

They wrapped scarves over their ears and noses, tucked hands into sleeves, and took the longest run of the morning. At the bottom, Marcus tumbled off, laughing, and reached up to test his ear. "Still there," he said. "Race you back to the top, one more, then Sofie's lobby for real."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Circuit diagrams show current flowing from positive to negative, but the electrons in the wires actually move from negative to positive.
story:
The shaded picnic table at the edge of the skate park had become Elena's study spot, because the library closed early on Saturdays and the ramps were loud but the tables were far enough away to think. She had a battery, a bulb, a switch, and three wires laid out on her science workbook, plus a note from her teacher, Mr. MacLeod, that had been plaguing her all morning. "Build it, then draw it," the note said, "arrows and all." Eason dropped his board on the bench across from her and watched her tape the wires down.

The first drawing was the problem. Her textbook showed arrows running from the positive end of the battery, through the switch, to the bulb, and back to negative. She copied it, then frowned. She clipped the wires exactly as the book showed, flipped the switch, and the bulb lit. Then she flipped through the chapter again and stopped at a line in small print that contradicted everything: the arrows in a diagram point one way, but the electrons actually go the other way, from negative to positive.

"That can't be right," she said. "The book says current flows positive to negative, but it also says the electrons move negative to positive." Eason leaned over the diagram. "So the arrows are backwards?" "No, the arrows are the convention. The electrons actually go the other way." She tested it the only way she could, by building the circuit twice, once matching the arrows and once flipped, and both times the bulb lit exactly the same, which meant the direction of the drawing didn't change what the electrons did, only the direction they truly moved did. Gianna rolled up from the bowl, heard the last part, and said, "So the picture lies on purpose?"

By late afternoon the sun had moved and the skaters had migrated to the ramps on the shady side, but Elena stayed at the table writing a text to Mr. MacLeod: "Built it. Bulb lights. Electrons go negative to positive, even though my arrows say positive to negative." She attached a photo of the glowing bulb sitting next to the diagram, then packed the wires into her pencil case and clipped the switch closed one more time so the bulb burned in the empty park behind her.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Looking at the horizon, a fixed distant point, can ease motion sickness because it helps the eyes agree with what the inner ear feels.
story:
The ferry to the island campground was crowded, and Brielle found a bench near the middle beside her friend Gabrielle. Cashton had claimed a seat by the window, but the windows were smeared with salt, so all he could see was a gray blur. Twenty minutes into the crossing, Gabrielle set down her snack bag and pressed both hands against her stomach. "I feel awful," she said. "The floor keeps moving."

Brielle looked at her. Then she looked at Cashton, who was playing a game on his phone, and back at Gabrielle, whose face had gone the color of the fog outside. Brielle remembered the summer before, when her mother had been queasy on a winding mountain road and had felt better as soon as they stopped at an overlook where she could stare at a far-off ridge. The difference was that her mother had been looking at something far away, while Gabrielle was staring at a bench, a floor, a snack bag, all close and all rocking. If a fixed distant point had helped, maybe a moving boat had the same rule.

"Come with me," Brielle said, and pulled Gabrielle toward the stairs. An impulsive passenger hurried past them with a coffee, and when he nearly knocked Gabrielle sideways, the deckhand stepped in to intervene and steered him toward the other rail. Brielle guided Gabrielle to the outer deck and pointed at the shoreline, a steady line of dark pines on the mainland. "Watch that. Don't look at the water."
Gabrielle kept her eyes on the trees. In a few minutes her shoulders loosened, and in a few more she said her stomach had settled. "The land isn't moving and the boat is," she said slowly, "but watching the land makes them agree somehow."

Cashton found them at the rail, holding his phone out toward the water. "Porpoise," he announced. "Two of them. Their skeletons are made of cartilage, not bone. I read the sign downstairs." Gabrielle laughed, took his phone, and photographed the porpoises herself, steady as anything, while the shoreline slid slowly past.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: Password-guessing programs try dictionary words, names, and common swaps like '@' for 'a' or '0' for 'o' early, so those swaps add little strength.
story:
Grace had the laptop open on the kitchen table when the message from Colt popped up on the screen: "guess what I made my new password. p@ssw0rd. replaced the a with @ and the o with 0. nobody will ever crack it."

Mahmoud, sitting across from her with a cookie in each hand, leaned over to read it. "He thinks he's a genius," he said.

Ms. Müller had lent them the password demo from computer club for the weekend, a program that did nothing but guess passwords, all afternoon if it had to, the way real guessing programs do. Grace had promised to return it Monday. She typed Colt's password into the box and pressed start. The counter blinked. The screen turned red and said CRACKED, and under it, almost instantly, the time appeared: less than one second. The red felt ominous, like a siren going off in the kitchen.

"That's because it guesses dictionary words and names first," Grace said slowly, watching the demo reset. "And it tries the swaps right after. @ for a, 0 for o. Everybody does those, so it checks them early." Mahmoud swallowed his cookie and slid the keyboard toward himself. "Okay, but what about my old one, SoccerRul3s?" Grace typed it in. Eight seconds. "Soccer's a word, and you only swapped the e." He stared at the red screen. "I use that everywhere. My game account, my email, everything."

Grace reassured him the way she'd want to be reassured. "We can fix it right now. Pick something that isn't a word at all." They made a deal, a settlement with real stakes: each of them would build a password, run it through the demo, and whoever's survived longer got the last cookie. Mahmoud typed "moose-banjo-lantern-fizz-42" and lasted past two minutes before Grace stopped the timer herself. Then he grabbed her phone and started typing a message to Colt. "Dear genius," he read aloud as he wrote, "your password lasted less than a second. Come over. Bring better ideas."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong; it is often written as "If... then..."
story:
Theo spread his supplies across the kitchen table and stared at the blank display board. The science fair was in three days, and all he had was a plastic prism he had won at the museum gift shop and one sentence written in his notebook: "Music is good for plants." His mom had leaned over his shoulder at breakfast and said it sounded nice. Nice was not going to win anything.

Casey arrived after lunch carrying a bag of sunflower seeds and half a sandwich he had no intention of sharing. "So you play music for a plant and then what?" Casey asked, chewing. "How do you know it was the music?" Theo opened his mouth, then closed it, because Casey was annoyingly right. If the plant grew, it might have grown anyway. "My cousin says a hypothesis has to be testable," Casey went on. "An experiment has to be able to prove you wrong." Theo wrote the word down. "So I need an if-then," he said slowly. "If I play music to one plant and not to another, and everything else is the same, then the music plant should grow differently." Casey saluted him with the sandwich.

They set up four cups of soil on the windowsill, two with music and two without, and Theo poked a drainage hole in each one so he could elaborate later about controlling the variables. Ms. Augustin, the neighbor whose garden stretched along the whole fence, lent him a watering cup marked in milliliters. "Same water, same light, same everything," she said, and winked. "That's what makes it science." She admired the prism sitting in the sunlight, throwing a small rainbow across the table, and called it exceptional, which Theo decided to put on the board as decoration even if it had nothing to do with plants.

By Friday the seeds had sprouted, and the music cups and the quiet cups were, annoyingly, almost identical in height. Theo measured twice, frowning, then shrugged and wrote it down anyway. On the display board, under the if-then sentence, he added his results in careful letters. Casey read it and grinned. "So music might do nothing." Theo propped the prism on the corner of the board, watched the rainbow land right on the word testable, and said, "Exactly. And that's the best part."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: Protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge, and neutrons have no charge at all.
story:
Kaylee spread the supplies across the kitchen table: three small bowls of beads, a bag of craft wire, and the assignment sheet Ms. Schneider had handed out that morning. Due tomorrow. Build a model of an atom with every particle in its right place. She had exactly one evening, a little homework money, and a mother who was already asking whether glitter counted as a science supply.

Kristian had come over to help, mostly because his own model was a lump of clay he called "an artistic interpretation." He poked through the bowls and frowned. "Okay, so red beads are protons, blue are neutrons, and yellow are electrons," he said. "Ms. Schneider said so, right? She wrote it on the board."

"She wrote the colors for protons and electrons," Kaylee said slowly, studying her notes. "Protons are positive, so they're red. Electrons are negative, so they're blue. Then neutrons are..." She stopped. Her notes just said "neutrons" with a question mark after it, because at that point Ms. Schneider had been telling Harman to stop drumming on his desk and Kaylee had looked up too late.

Kristian shrugged. "So make them yellow. What's the difference?"

"But yellow means something in the code," Kaylee said. "Every other color on that board means something. If neutrons are yellow, people will think they have some charge we forgot to write down." She turned a bead over in her fingers, thinking out loud. "Protons are positive. Electrons are negative. So neutrons have to be..." She tested the idea against the board in her memory, the way you check a puzzle piece against the picture on the box. "Nothing. Neutrons have no charge at all."

"So use a color that means nothing," Kristian said.

They dug through the craft box and found white beads, plain and blank as an unpainted wall. Kaylee wired the nucleus first, packing red and white beads tight together in the center, then curved three wire orbits around it for the blue electrons. The wire kept slipping, so she wrapped the joints in little sleeves of tape, which insulated them from each other and held everything steady. Kristian, who turned out to be surprisingly good with pliers, twisted each orbit into a perfect circle and announced, "I'm basically an artisan."

"It's one atom," Kaylee said, but she was smiling.

The next morning Ms. Schneider walked the rows, pausing at Kaylee's model. She picked it up, tilted it toward the window, and read the little label taped to the base: "White means no charge." Her eyebrows went up.

"Most of the class made neutrons yellow," she said. "Half of them decided neutrons must be negative, because negative sounds like neutral. You caught the trap."

Behind her, Harman was scowling at his model, pulling yellow beads off a lopsided nucleus. "Ironic," he muttered. "I spent the longest on mine and it's the wrongest one here."

Kaylee slid her bead box across the aisle to him. "White ones," she said. "Start over. I have plenty."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: In staggered breathing, choir members take breaths at different moments, so a long note keeps sounding even though every singer breathes.
story:
John had sung the low part all afternoon in Grandpa's front room, and every time the long note came, he ruined it. Frank held the high line just fine, but when John ran out of air and gulped, the bottom of the sound dropped away, and the whole thing collapsed like one of Grandpa's model bridges.

"Again," said Frank, grinning, which made John want to conquer the note right there on the spot. They were practicing for the spring concert, where the choir would sing in two-part harmony, and the low part had to hold against the high part even when it felt like his lungs were empty paper bags.

Grandpa sat in his armchair putting together a little plastic car, snapping intricate pieces of some polymer kit together while the boys sang. The second time they failed, he held up one hand. "Let me record you," he said, and set his phone on the table before John could argue.

They sang it once more, John breathing in the same wrong spot, and Grandpa played it back. John leaned close to the phone. There it was, his gasp, ugly and obvious. But he noticed something else, something he hadn't heard while singing. On the recording, the sound never fully stopped. It went thin for a moment, then filled back out. He frowned and tapped the screen. "Play the long note again." He listened twice, three times, with his eyes shut.

"Frank," he said slowly, "you breathe before I do. We're not breathing at the same time." They tried it on purpose, and it worked even better. When John breathed, Frank's note carried, and when Frank breathed, John's was there. Ainsley arrived just then with the sheet music, and John pulled her into the room. "We figured it out. We take breaths at different moments, so the note keeps sounding even though every singer breathes. Mr. Khan never even told us that."

"Then sing it for me," Ainsley said, and stood by the window to listen.

The note stretched out long and steady under their voices, and outside, a bird answered it.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
story:
Samanthal knelt beside the campfire ring, holding a lumpy ball of dough that refused to puff. "Come on," she whispered to it. "Do your job." Her family's tent flapped in the morning draft, and somewhere behind the trailers a generator droned like a sleepy dragon, but none of that mattered. What mattered was that she had promised everyone fresh bread tonight, and her dough lay in the bowl looking as lethargic as her brother before breakfast, flat and lazy and completely unrisen.

She pulled a folded letter from her jacket pocket, the one her friend Layne had mailed her the day before camp started. "Dear Samantha," it read, "my grandma taught me bread this summer. Her three rules: give the yeast sugar to eat, keep the water warm like bathwater, not hot like tea, and never rush it. Hunter says bread is alive, which is creepy and also true. Bake something amazing. Your friend, Layne." Samantha read it twice. Bathwater, not tea. She closed her eyes and remembered standing in Mr. Addo's kitchen last spring, helping him knead his famous Saturday loaves. He had let her stick a finger in the water before it went into the bowl, and it had felt like nothing at all, just pleasantly warm. But this morning, she had poured the water straight off the camp stove because she was in a hurry, and it had steamed.

"So it's the yeast," she said out loud. "The hot water did something to it." She thought about what Layne's letter had said about sugar, and about Hunter's creepy idea that bread was alive, and she pieced it together. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles," she told the dough sternly, as if scolding it. If the yeast was ruined, there would be no bubbles, and no bubbles meant no puffy loaf. She had a theory, and she could test it. She filled the water pot again, warmed it gently, touched it with her finger the way Mr. Addo had shown her, and started a fresh batch with a new packet of yeast and a spoonful of sugar from the supply box.

An hour later, Hunter's little brother, who was camping two sites over, wandered by and peered into her bowl. "It grew," he said, sounding personally offended. "Like a balloon." Samantha grinned and punched the dough down, watching it sigh flat again, then shaped it into a round loaf and set it in the dutch oven by the coals. Her mother had said camp bread was impossible and they should just eat sandwiches. When Samantha lifted the lid later and the smell of warm, crusty bread rolled out into the trees, her mother took a bite, closed her eyes, and said, "I was wrong. I am officially changing my mind about everything."

"Even about my tree house plans?" Samantha asked. Her mother handed her another slice and said, "Draft me a proposal tonight."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
The line outside the mall's game store stretched past the fountain and curved toward the pretzel stand. Sofia held her sixty dollars in a zipped pocket and counted the people ahead of her, thirty-two at least. Giselle and Ireland had saved spots near the front, and when Sofia reached them, Ireland was bouncing on her toes.

"They're selling the new star fox plush for twelve dollars today only," Ireland said. "The toy store two floors up has the same one for thirty."

"Then why would anyone buy it up there?" Sofia asked.

"Because down here they sell out," Giselle said. "Last month it was the dragon plush. Gone in four minutes. My brother says the store keeps the price too low, so everybody wants one, and there aren't enough to go around. He says that's called a shortage."

At ten o'clock the doors opened, and the line contracted into a tight crowd at the register. Sofia watched the shelf of silver foxes through the glass. A clerk carried out one box, then another, and then he shook his head and held up his empty hands. Sofia was still nine people from the front. Around her, fans groaned and checked their phones. A boy near the counter said he'd been waiting since seven.

Sofia turned her logic over as the crowd broke apart. Twelve dollars, three hundred people, maybe sixty plushes. Thirty dollars, and upstairs she'd seen rows of them sitting untouched on a shelf. The price was the difference. When the plush was cheap, more people wanted it than there were plushes to sell. When it cost more, plenty sat waiting. She pictured the two shelves like symmetrical mirrors, one empty and one crowded, and wondered whether the same rule worked for other things.

"Let's test it," she said. "The pretzel stand sells plain pretzels for a dollar and there's a whole rack. The cinnamon ones are four dollars and there's always a line."

They walked over. The rack of plain pretzels stood full and steaming, and only one customer stood there. At the cinnamon window, six people waited while a fresh tray came out and vanished in under two minutes. Ireland watched the last cinnamon pretzel leave with its buyer and nodded slowly. "Same thing," she said. "Cheap and scarce, or pricey and plentiful."

They rode the escalator to the toy store, where Ms. Cho was straightening a display. Sofia walked to the shelf and counted eleven silver foxes, glossy and identical, each with a thirty-dollar tag. She had enough. She picked one up, and the fur was softer than she'd imagined.

"Changed my mind," Ireland said behind her, grabbing one too. "Waiting in line at dawn is not worth it. I'd rather pay more and actually get the fox."

Sofia carried hers to the register and set her sixty dollars on the counter. "One fox, please," she said.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
Megan had taped a growth chart to the back of her bedroom door, and every Friday night she stood against it with a pencil while her dog watched from the rug. Nothing. The same pencil mark for three weeks. She was eleven and a half, and she had a theory: something invisible was happening to her, something working underneath like seeds waiting to germinate, and if she could just find the pattern, she would know when to expect things.

That Friday, her classmate Baby came over with a sleeping bag and a letter she refused to open. "It's from my sister," Baby said, dropping it on the bed. "She's away at camp. I'm saving it for later because if it's bad news I want to still have a good evening first." Megan respected that logic, and they ate popcorn and painted their toes instead.

Later, in the dark, Baby finally opened it by flashlight. "She says her bunkmate got her first period and cried, and the counselor says it's normal at twelve. That's the middle, she wrote. Half of girls get it before twelve and half after." Megan sat up. Her own older cousin had gotten hers at ten, which had scared Megan into thinking she was late. "So it's not a race," Megan said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "There's a whole range around twelve, and everyone lands somewhere in it." She felt something settle, like a rule she had finally proven. "My cousin was just at one end."

"So it's like an ecosystem," Baby said, waving the flashlight. "Everybody's on their own schedule, but it all still works." Megan laughed and wrote the rule on an index card and taped it beside the growth chart: not late, not early, somewhere in a wide normal range.

In the morning Baby's nerves had turned into excitement, which was contagious, and the two of them ran the experiment one more time. Megan stood against the door, and Baby drew a careful new line. "Up a quarter inch," Baby announced, tapping the chart. "See? Something's been happening all along."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Emma had promised Ms. Xu a bar graph of her town's ethnic and cultural origins by Monday, and the numbers would not behave. She spread her survey papers across the kitchen table while the relatives talked over the spaghetti. The percentages from the town's census website added up to one hundred and thirty-two percent, which was impossible, and Emma despised impossible numbers more than anything else on a homework sheet.

"Something's wrong with the data," she told her cousin, who was stacking garlic bread like a wall. Emma narrowed her eyes at the page. Either the census people couldn't do arithmetic, or something was hiding in the numbers, some rule she hadn't figured out yet. She decided to test it the only way she could, with the people in this very room.

She grabbed a notepad and worked the long table like a game show host. "Grandma, where's your family from?" "Italy," Grandma said, "and your grandfather's side is Scottish." Uncle Ray raised his fork. "Filipino and Irish. Ask me about the monsoon season sometime, I was born during one." Auntie Priya laughed. "Indian and Ukrainian, and before you ask, yes, my mother makes competent samosas and competent perogies." Emma wrote it all down, then counted. Eleven people at the table. Fifteen origins in her tally. She flipped the page over and did the math again, because fifteen origins from eleven people meant her little survey would show over one hundred percent too, if she graphed it the way she had graphed the town.

She texted her classmate Dorian, who loved census facts the way other kids loved hockey stats. His reply came fast: "Its not a mistake. Since 1981 Canada's census lets people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population." Emma read it twice, then looked at Grandma, then at her tally sheet, and felt the hidden rule click into place like the last piece of a puzzle. The town's numbers weren't broken. They were extra full, the way this table was extra full.

She redrew the graph that evening, adding a note in her best printing: Origins add up to more than one hundred percent because people belong to more than one. Then she added a small legend, using her own family, just for Ms. Xu: Italian, Scottish, Filipino, Irish, Indian, Ukrainian, all in one kitchen.

Madelynn texted a picture of her own graph, which also went over one hundred, with the message "MINE IS BROKEN TOO."

"Mine was," Emma typed back. "Bring your markers tomorrow."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Ancient Egyptians divided the year into three seasons based on the Nile: Akhet, the flood; Peret, the growing season; and Shemu, the harvest.
story:
Aurora spread the scraps of papyrus-colored paper across the archive table and glared at them. The city archive smelled like dust and old glue, and Mr. Iyer had said she could stay until closing if she kept quiet, which was hard, because her class calendar project was falling apart. Four seasons, spring, summer, fall, winter. That was how calendars worked. But every book she pulled from the Egypt boxes insisted the ancient year had three seasons, and no book said why. "Maybe the books are biased," she whispered to Erin, who was drawing crocodiles on the margin of their poster. "Maybe whoever wrote them just liked the number three."

"Or maybe you just can't count," said Barrett, sliding into the chair beside her with a box labeled NILE RECORDS. He dumped it out, and out tumbled photographs of the river, month by month, taken over decades for the city's flood maps. Aurora flipped through them slowly. In some, the river lapped high over its banks, drowning the fields. In others, the same fields stood green and striped with crops. In the last ones, workers bent low, cutting grain. She laid three photos side by side. Flood. Growing. Harvest. Then she counted the months on the flood maps and matched them against the photographs, and her pencil hovered over the paper.

She wrote three columns instead of four. At the top of the first she put the word she had found on a museum card: "Akhet." The second she labeled "Peret." The third, "Shemu."

"That's the flood, the growing season, and the harvest," Aurora said, tapping each column. "That's why three. The river did the counting." She wanted to incorporate the whole thing into the calendar before anyone could argue, so she grabbed the glue before Erin could draw another crocodile on it. Barrett leaned over her shoulder, read the labels, and frowned. "Then where's winter?" Aurora opened her mouth, then closed it. She picked up her pencil and wrote, small, in the corner of the poster: "No snow. Not one flake. Barrett checked."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
story:
Brielle sat at the kitchen table with her cast propped on a pillow, staring at the drawing she had made of her own arm bone. Three days ago the doctor had told her mother that the break missed the growth plate, and everyone had smiled, but nobody had said why that was good news. Brielle wanted to know. She had drawn a long bone and put little squiggles near both ends, because she remembered the doctor pointing to the ends when she said it.

Faisal came in through the back door carrying a jar of beans. "My bean project," he said, setting it down beside the fruit bowl. "I want mine to germinate first out of the whole class. I'm putting them on your windowsill because your kitchen gets the best sun." He wet a paper towel and folded the beans inside the jar, then turned it so the light hit it.

"That peach is going to ruin your beans," Brielle said. The peach in the bowl had a gray patch spreading across its skin. "That's fungus. My mom says one bad piece can spread to everything touching it." Faisal made a face and carried the peach to the compost bucket under the sink.

Then he leaned over her drawing. "Why does your arm bone have scribbles at the ends?"

"I think I figured it out," Brielle said. She tapped the squiggles. "Those are growth plates. That's what the doctor called them, at the ends of long bones. They're made of cartilage, and that's where the bone lengthens while you're a kid. If a break goes right through one, it can affect how the bone grows after that." She traced her cast with her finger. "Mine didn't, which is why everyone smiled."

"So how do you know it's still growing in there?" Faisal asked.

"I measured my other arm with the tape measure this morning," Brielle said. "I wrote the number in my notebook. I'm going to measure again next week and the week after, and if the number gets bigger, then the growth plates are working. Same as your beans."

Faisal grinned and slid the jar next to her notebook. "Then we'll watch both experiments at once."

Brielle picked up her pencil and wrote "ARM: 46 CENTIMETERS" across the top of a fresh page, then drew an arrow pointing at the bean jar.

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: Tightening a string raises its pitch and loosening it lowers the pitch.
story:
Scarlett held the borrowed guitar up to her ear and plucked the fat E string, and the note wobbled like a door that needed oil. Mr. Dlamini had left the music room door open with a sign taped to it that said TUNING PRACTICE, COME IN, along with a small silver pitch pipe. He had played one low note on the pipe before heading down the hall. "Match that," he had said. "By Friday."

The problem was that Scarlett had no idea which way to turn the peg. She remembered last summer at Theodore's grandparents' house, when he had cranked a peg with total confidence and the note sank lower and lower, like a whale diving. Theodore had insisted the guitar was broken. His grandfather had laughed until he had to sit down. Scarlett turned the peg the opposite way from what Theodore had done, just a tiny bit, and plucked again. The note crept upward.

"Is that right?" Marko leaned in the doorway, holding a sandwich he clearly wanted to eat more than anything, since lunch was in ten minutes and he had skipped breakfast. He had come to complain to Mr. Dlamini about the chess club schedule, but the room had a pull on him. "It sounds less like a dying animal now. Progress."

Scarlett plucked the string, then blew the pitch pipe and plucked again, back and forth until the two notes sat together like matching socks. The old strings felt brittle under her fingers, dry as autumn leaves, and she worried that one wrong twist might snap one. She loosened the next string a little too far, heard it dive, and brought it back up again, more slowly this time. If turning one way raised a note and the other way lowered it, she could fix any mistake. She only had to listen.

By the time the bell rang, four strings rang true and the fifth was close. Marko had eaten the sandwich, crumbs down his shirt, and was strumming the air like a rock star. "Teach me that tomorrow," he said, "and I'll trade you my seat by the window on the bus." Scarlett looked at the guitar, at the little silver pipe, and shook the last string's note upward until it locked into place. "Deal," she said, and blew the pipe one more time to check.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
Amelia stood on Aurora's porch holding a wrapped box of mangoes, her gift clutched so tight the ribbon crinkled. Aurora's grandmother had moved in last month from Chiang Mai, and Aurora had invited her over to meet him... no, her. Amelia had practiced the greeting on the walk: press your palms together, bow slightly, say "sawasdee khrap" if you were a boy and "sawasdee kha" if you were a girl. She was a girl, so "kha" it was.

The door opened and a small woman in a blue blouse smiled up at her. Amelia pressed her palms together, bowed, and said "sawasdee kha." The grandmother's face lit up like a struck match, and she returned the gesture and said something warm and quick that Amelia couldn't follow. Aurora pulled her inside by the sleeve. "That was so good," she whispered. "She'll like you forever now."

The living room had a low table already set with bowls, and a canopy of paper lanterns hung from the ceiling, strung by Aurora's dad for the occasion. Amelia handed the gift across with both hands, the way she'd read you should, and the grandmother took it with both hands too and set it aside unopened. Amelia felt a jolt of worry. She had expected thank-yous, maybe some unwrapping. Why set it down like that? She watched, waiting. Aurora's dad disappeared into the kitchen, came back, called everyone to the table, and only then did the grandmother quietly pick the box up again and place it somewhere careful, near a small shelf with a framed photograph. Amelia began to form a guess: gifts here were not opened in front of the giver. She decided to test it by watching what happened with Aurora's present later. Sure enough, when Aurora's dad handed over a small bag of sweets, the grandmother thanked him, smiled, and set it by the box. Nobody opened anything.

At dinner Amelia kept noticing small rules. The grandmother served the eldest person first, and everyone waited until Aurora's dad lifted his spoon before eating. Aurora leaned close. "Watch this," she murmured, and pointed at her little cousin, a boy of about five who was stacking rice into a tower. Amelia reached over to ruffle his hair affectionately, the way her own uncle always did to her, and Aurora caught her wrist. "Don't. In Thailand the head is sacred. Touching someone's head, even just to pat a kid, is rude there."

Amelia pulled her hand back slowly. The rule was invisible, but the evidence had been everywhere once she looked: the grandmother's quick sidestep earlier when a visitor had reached toward the boy, the way she touched her own head and then her chest as if apologizing for something. Amelia had dismissed that little dance as a stretch. It hadn't been.

"Even for someone as sophisticated as you," the grandmother said in careful English, catching Amelia's wide eyes, "new rules take time." Then she spooned a second helping of rice onto Amelia's plate and gestured for her to eat.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Lines of longitude meet at the poles, so a degree of longitude spans about 111 kilometers at the equator but shrinks to zero at the poles.
story:
The flight to Denver was delayed, which meant Samantha's class trip had turned into two hours of airport chairs, and Gillian had already eaten both her granola bars. Ms. Russo had handed out atlases to keep everyone busy, and Samantha's job was to find the class destination using latitude and longitude. She traced her finger along the lines until it landed on the dot with the airport code.

"There," she said. "Thirty-nine point seven north, one hundred four point nine west. That's us, flying almost to the middle."

Gillian leaned over. "Why are the lines all squished together at the top? Did somebody smash the map?"

Samantha squinted. The longitude lines, straight and evenly spaced at the equator, bunched tighter and tighter toward the top of the globe, like ribs on an accordion. She tested one with her thumb, measuring the gap between two lines at the equator, then sliding her thumb upward. The gap shrank under her finger.

"Look at this," she said. "A degree here is fat. A degree up there is skinny."

"So a degree isn't always the same size?" Gillian frowned at the page. "That's like a ruler that changes its mind."

"It's like lines of longitude meet at the poles," Samantha said slowly, watching the lines converge at the very top. "A degree of longitude spans about a hundred and eleven kilometers at the equator, but it shrinks to zero at the poles."

"Zero," Gillian repeated. "So at the pole, you could walk across every time zone in one step?" She stood up and demonstrated, stomping in a tiny circle. "I'm in Denver. Now I'm in London. Now I'm somewhere with penguins."

"You'd flourish there," Samantha said. "You've already eaten everything in this time zone."

A shop clerk passing by with a cart glanced at them and smiled. Ms. Russo looked up from her coffee. "Finding Denver?"

"Found it," Samantha said, tapping the dot. "And lost about a hundred and eleven kilometers on the way."

Gillian pointed at the snack stand. "Then let's go find those pretzels before they shrink to zero too."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
story:
Parker squeezed past a row of knees holding two hot chocolates, one for himself and one for his little sister, who had been shivering in her thin jacket since the second inning. He had budgeted his allowance for weeks to afford seats like these, close enough to see the stitches on the ball, and now the whole family was here plus Nick and Elias from his class. Below them the crowd roared as the home team's shortstop turned a double play, and Parker nearly wore both drinks.

"How does he do that?" Elias said, leaning forward. "That was so fast."

"He's just competent," Nick said, shrugging. "Like, actually competent. Some guys are fast and some guys just know where to be."
