Parker was half listening. Something was nagging at him, and he scanned the field, jersey by jersey. Three. Seven. Twenty-one. Five. Eleven. He checked the visiting team's dugout too. Nobody, on either side, wore 42. "Hey," he said. "Look at the numbers. Nobody out there has forty-two. Not one player."

Elias squinted at the field. "Maybe it's bad luck?"

"It's not bad luck," Parker said slowly. "It's on purpose. It has to be." He turned the idea over. If one team skipped a number, fine, superstition. But both teams, every player? That sounded like a rule. He tested it in his head: Mariano Rivera, the Yankees closer, his dad talked about him all the time. Rivera wore 42. So it wasn't banned forever. He dug the program out from under his seat and flipped through the team pages, running his finger down the rosters. Number 42 was simply missing, like a tooth knocked out of a smile.

Nick pulled out his phone while Elias shielded the screen from the glare. "Okay, okay, it says here... in 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete was honored that way. Every team. The whole league."

"Retired it," Parker repeated, and the word felt heavy and good in his mouth, like something an emperor would command. Nobody could ever wear it again except the few already wearing it when the rule came. "So Rivera was grandfathered in. That's why I remembered it." He nudged his sister, who was still shivering, and draped his own jacket over her shoulders even though the night air bit. "Robinson," he said. "That's why it's everybody, not just one team."

The crowd rose around them as the closer struck out the side, and Parker stood up too, jacket-less and grinning, cup held high.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: The graph of an equation like y = 2x + 1 is always a straight line, so plotting just two correct points is enough to draw it with a ruler.
story:
Julia pressed her pencil so hard against the grid paper that the tip snapped. Across the room, the clock above Mr. Georgiou's whiteboard showed only four minutes left in math club, and she had plotted exactly one point for y = 2x + 1.

"When x is one, y is three," she muttered, marking the point. "But we're supposed to show the whole equation, and I've got one dot."

Libby leaned over from the next desk. "I did three points and it took me forever. There's no way you finish."

Julia could perceive the shape forming on Libby's page, though: three dots in a row, all lined up like fence posts. One more point, and a ruler could connect them. But was two enough? She had never tested that. Quickly, she chose x is zero, worked out that y must be one, and plotted the second point beside the first.

She laid her ruler across both dots and drew the line, then stopped. It looked right, but she needed to check. She picked x is three, calculated y is seven, and placed a small circle on the line. It landed exactly on her ruler's edge. She tried x is negative one, and that point sat on the line too, like it had been waiting there.

"Every single one," Julia whispered.

"Every single one what?" Izaak asked, sliding his chair over.

"Every point I test lands on the line, even though I only drew it through two points. So plotting two correct points is enough. You don't need more."

"Two?" Izaak squinted at her paper. "That feels like cheating."

"It's not cheating, it's faster. Try it." She handed him her ruler, its edge still warm from her hand. Mr. Georgiou had begun collecting papers, and the room smelled of pencil shavings and the oranges he kept on his desk. Julia slid her sheet to the front, a genuine solution with a line running clean across the grid.

Next week, she decided, she would show Izaak an adaptation of her shortcut: two points, one ruler, and half the time to spare. "Bring your own ruler," she told him. "Mine's got tooth marks."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wet snow near the freezing point packs into snowballs well because it holds a thin layer of liquid water, while very cold, dry snow crumbles.
story:
The snow came down overnight with no warning at all, and by morning the radio said school was closed. Charlie texted Mack, and they met at ten o'clock in Riverside Park, where the playground looked like a frosted cake.

"Snowman," Mack said, and scooped up two armfuls of powder. Charlie tried to pack hers into a ball, but the snow fell apart between her mittens like sugar. She tried again, pressing harder, and it crumbled even faster.

"It's too fluffy," Mack said, kicking at it. "Look, it won't even stick to itself."

Charlie sat back on her heels and thought. Yesterday the freezing rain had turned to snow, and this morning the thermometer on her kitchen window read just under freezing, near thirty-two degrees. But the snow felt dry and squeaky, more like the cold snaps in January than like today. She remembered last year, when they had made perfect snowballs in the afternoon after the sun had been on the field for hours. Back then the snow had felt almost damp, and it had packed so hard that Mack's brother complained it was "basically ice."

"Maybe it needs to warm up a little," Charlie said. "Last year's good snow felt wetter than this."

"Wetter snow sounds worse," Mack said.

"Maybe not. Maybe wet snow near freezing sticks together, and dry snow like this crumbles." She stood up. "Let's wait for the sun to do its work, then test it."

They sledded down the hill by the baseball diamond while they waited. Near the fence, an old man grumbled to his dog about the sidewalk, saying the landlord never shoveled it, and that a negligent landlord was going to get somebody hurt. Charlie dragged her sled around the icy patch carefully. By one o'clock the sun was bright on the open field, and she noticed her boot prints looked shiny and damp.

She grabbed a handful and squeezed. The snow held. She tossed a test ball against the fence, and it thumped instead of bursting.

"Wet snow near freezing packs," Charlie said, grinning. "Dry cold snow just crumbles. Come on!"

They rolled the bottom ball together, then the middle, then the head, and Charlie ran to find two pebbles for eyes before the light changed.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: Municipalities that allow delegations usually require people to register with the city clerk's office before the meeting.
story:
Rebecca had read the bylaw three times on the bus, and it still said the same tedious thing: no bikes allowed on the riverside path. She and Bentley rode that path every Saturday, and now they would have to push their bikes through gravel beside it. "We're going to the town hall meeting tonight," she told him at lunch. "We'll speak to the council and get it changed." Bentley's own wish was smaller and sharper; he wanted to be the one who talked, because he had never spoken into a real microphone before and it felt like an audition for something bigger.

The hall smelled like coffee and floor wax. Rows of folding chairs, a long table up front, and five councillors who looked tired already. When the meeting opened, a woman from the gardening club stood up, clutching a stack of notes, and asked to speak about the flower beds by the library. The clerk at the side table shook her head. "I'm sorry. Delegations have to register with the city clerk's office before the meeting."

The woman sat down, deflated, and Rebecca felt her stomach drop. She nudged Bentley. "Before the meeting. Nobody told us that." She watched the clerk flip through a binder and noticed the page had names on it, printed neatly, with times beside each one. So the order of speakers was set before anyone even walked in. That meant their plan had a hidden step they had skipped.

Rebecca raised her hand. When the mayor nodded at her, she kept her voice steady. "We're not registered, but can we sign up for the next meeting tonight, so we don't miss it again?" The clerk smiled a little and slid a form across the table. "You can fill that in now," she said, "and you'll be first on the list for next month." Bentley leaned over the form, gripping the pen. "I'll do the talking part," he whispered. "You did the figuring-out part."

Rebecca inhaled the coffee smell one more time, wrote their names in block letters, and slid the form back across the table.

"See you next month," the clerk said.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Double-acting baking powder releases gas twice: once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven.
story:
Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it again, because last time he had skipped that step and the muffins had rebelled, flat and gray as river stones. This time he turned the dial to preheat the oven first, measured the flour, and cracked the eggs. Noemy leaned against the fridge with her phone ready, because she wanted a photo of a perfect muffin for the baking club page, and her last three attempts had looked like accidents. "You get one shot at mine," Nolan warned her. "Then you owe me a muffin," she said.

The recipe said to fill the cups and bake right away, but halfway through spooning batter, the doorbell rang. Jimmy stood there holding a frail paper bag that had torn at the bottom, spilling three marbles onto the step. While Nolan helped him gather them, he kept glancing back at the kitchen, where the bowl of batter sat waiting on the counter.

He remembered the Saturday his grandmother let him stir while she talked. "It's double-acting," she had said, tapping the tin of baking powder. "It releases gas twice, once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven." He had nodded without really listening, too busy licking the spoon. Now he stared at the resting batter and thought about that. If the first gas had already fizzled out while he chased marbles, the muffins would be flat, and Noemy's photo would be another disaster. But if the second release was still waiting for the oven's heat, maybe the batter could afford to sit for a few minutes, exactly like the recipe seemed to hint when it said not to worry about the last few cups.

"That's the buzzer," Noemy called from the kitchen. Nolan slid the tray in, set the timer, and wiped his hands on the towel. "If they come out flat," he said, "I'm blaming your club photo." Twenty minutes later he pulled the tray out, and the muffins stood tall and golden, tops cracked like little mountains. Noemy snapped three pictures before he even set the tray down. "Tallest one is mine," Jimmy said, reaching past him.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Theodor's little brother was home from school with an ear infection, so the two of them were stuck inside on a rainy Saturday, sharing Theodor's phone on the living room floor. They had already scrolled past what felt like a thousand photos, so many pictures of migratory birds that the screen seemed saturated with feathers, because Theodor's science project on bird migration was due Monday.

"Let's search ourselves," Theodor said, grinning. "Everybody does it." He typed his own name first and found nothing but a runner from another country. Then Liam took the phone and typed Liam plus his last name. The second result made his stomach drop. It was a comment he had written two whole years ago, on a public video about their town's skate park, back when he thought only his friends would ever see it. It said the park was boring and so was the coach who ran it, and it still had his full name attached, sitting there for anyone in the world to read.

"How is it still there?" Liam whispered. "That was forever ago." Theodor shrugged and scrolled, but Liam kept thinking, turning the problem over the way he did with math puzzles. His mom had said once that search engines copy public pages using automated programs called crawlers. If a crawler had copied his comment, then it lived somewhere he couldn't see, like a photocopy stuck in a drawer he couldn't open. He tested the idea: he searched the exact words from his comment, without his name. The comment came up again, third result. So it wasn't connected to his name only. It was public, copied, indexed, findable.

He clicked through until he reached the video page and found a delete button next to his own words. His thumb hovered. The coach from the skate park had helped him land his first ollie last summer, before Liam even knew they had met before. He pressed delete, and the comment vanished from the page. Then he typed his own name into the search bar one more time, just to see, and exhaled slowly at what came up on the screen.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
story:
Emily slid her French worksheet across the library table and read it a third time. Ms. Nowak's assignment was printed at the top: describe your family and pets in full sentences, in French. Around her, the library hummed with whispers and page turns, and Koen was already halfway down his page, writing fast, which worried her because Koen never checked anything.

"Ma mère a un chat," Emily said under her breath, testing it. My mother has a cat. That one felt solid. She kept going. "Mon frère a deux poissons." Her brother had two fish, a reckless pair who once leapt from their tank and survived because her mother happened to walk past. Writing about them was easy. Then she reached the last line, the one Ms. Nowak had circled twice: tell your own age and your family's ages.

She wrote "Je suis douze ans" and stopped. Something about it snagged in her mind like a sleeve on a nail. She flipped through her notebook to the vocab list. Avoir, to have. Être, to be. Two different verbs, and she had just used the wrong one, she was almost sure, though she couldn't see why she was sure. It was like guessing a fish was sick because it stopped swimming, without ever seeing the sickness itself.

Koen leaned over. "Stuck on the age part too?"

"I think there's a pattern," Emily said. "I just can't see it yet." She grabbed a scrap paper and started collecting evidence like a detective. Their textbook's sample dialogue said "J'ai treize ans" for one character. A photo caption said "Elle a neuf ans." A workbook answer key, which Ms. Nowak had left on the cart, said "Tu as quel âge?" Every single one used avoir. To have. Emily felt the pattern click into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. "They say it with have, not with am. J'ai douze ans. It means 'I am twelve,' but word for word it says 'I have twelve years.'"

Koen stared at his own page. "I wrote 'Je suis onze ans.'" He erased it so hard the paper thinned, and the torn corner drifted to the floor. Emily pulled out her pen and wrote her sentence again, cleanly this time, then added her mother's age and her brother's age, all with avoir, all with years.

"One more sentence," Koen said. "The pets."

Emily grinned and wrote, "Mes poissons sont les seuls organismes dans notre maison qui ne crient jamais," then translated for him: my fish are the only organisms in our house who never shout. Koen laughed, but quietly, because Ms. Nowak was already walking their way, holding the stack of corrected tests. She set Emily's last quiz face down on the table and moved on without a word. Emily turned it over slowly, and there, in red ink beside her sentence about age, was a note: "See me. Almost right."

She looked at her new sentence, then at the quiz, then back at her new sentence. "Koen," she whispered, "watch the door. I'm going to try the avoir rule one more time before she comes back."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
story:
Arianna had been stuck home for four days with the flu, and today was the deadline: her science fair project, the one she'd been building out of painted cardboard, was due at school by three o'clock, and the doctor's appointment her mother had booked for eleven was the only thing standing between her and the door. At the clinic, Ms. Ferreira, the pharmacist behind the small counter near the waiting room, was sorting bottles while a boy about Arianna's age clutched a wad of bright green tissues and announced that he definitely needed the strong medicine because his snot was green.

"Green means infection, right?" the boy said, his voice brittle with worry.

Arianna sat up. She'd been staring at her own crumpled tissues all week, thinking the same thing. Ms. Ferreira shook her head. "The color comes from your immune cells and an enzyme they release," she said. "It doesn't tell you if it's bacteria or a virus."

The boy frowned. Arianna's mind started turning. If color didn't tell you the cause, then everyone who panicked at green tissues was panicking for nothing, and that included her, because she'd been saving her grossest tissue in a zip bag, planning to show the doctor as proof she needed something strong. She had been incorporating that tissue into her whole plan, like evidence in a trial. She looked at the boy's pale face and the way he kept checking the clock above the counter, probably late for something too.

"Want to test it?" she whispered to him. She held up her bag. "Mine's been green since Tuesday, and I only have a virus, the doctor said so on Monday. Two green samples, two different causes, so the color can't be the thing that tells them apart." The boy's shoulders dropped with relief. He smiled, wadded his tissues into his pocket, and walked out with his dad instead of demanding medicine.

When the nurse finally called her name, Arianna left the zip bag on her chair. On the way out, she caught the boy's eye through the window and waved her project box. "Good luck!" she called through the glass.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Evan had never been so nervous about noodles. His mom's coworker, Mr. Iyer, had invited their whole family to a gathering at his sister's house, and somehow Evan had ended up at the ramen table beside Mr. Iyer's Japanese son-in-law, with a bowl of steaming broth in front of him and absolutely no plan.

The problem was the noise. The moment everyone started eating, the room filled with slurps, big wet ropey ones, coming from every side of the table. Evan froze with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth. At home, slurping meant somebody got the Look, the one that could diminish your dessert to zero in a single glance. His bias said loud eaters were rude eaters, and his brain was screaming that rule at him right now.

"Ramen's better hot," the son-in-law said, then slurped again, cheerfully, like it was music. "You have to hurry."

Evan watched him, then watched Mr. Iyer's sister doing exactly the same thing, then a grandmother down the table doing it loudest of all. Nobody flinched. Nobody gave anyone the Look. So maybe, he reasoned, the rule wasn't about noise at all, it was about where you were sitting. He decided to run a test. He lifted a tangle of noodles, took a breath, and slurped as hard as he could.

It worked. The noodles actually tasted better, cooler and faster, and a fleck of broth flew up and landed on his own forehead, which made a little kid across the table laugh so hard she had to put her spoon down.

"Excellent slurp," the son-in-law said, thumping him on the shoulder. "Better than mine."

"Impossible," said Evan, already going back in for round two. He was, after all, a very frugal eater when ramen was involved, and he didn't intend to waste a single noodle or a single second being polite about it.

story:
Christopher sat on Brennan's kitchen floor while Brennan's dad set the small box on the counter, and he could hardly keep his hands still. Tomorrow was his own phone day, but tonight he got to practice on Brennan's, because Brennan had promised to teach him the rules before he broke any of them by accident.

"Rule one," Brennan said, holding the phone up like a trophy. "Never text during dinner. Rule two, actually read what you typed before you send it."

"I already know those," Christopher said. "I want to know how they work. Like, how long have people even carried phones around? Did cave people have them?"

Brennan laughed so hard he slid into the cabinet. Then he stopped, because he actually knew. "We had this poster in Ms. Chowdhury's class last year. It had a picture of a man on a New York street, April 3, 1973, holding this giant brick thing. It was the first call ever made from a handheld cellular phone. His name was Martin Cooper, and he was an engineer at Motorola."

"From a street?" Christopher stared at the phone in Brennan's hand. "So nobody had a pocket phone before that?"

"Fifty-something years ago, that was the very first one. Everybody else was stuck at home."

Christopher decided to test this. He typed a message to Theodor, who was home with a cold: "Did you know the first handheld cell call was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973?" Then, after a moment, he added, "Feel better. Can you send me a photo of that poster in Ms. Chowdhury's room?"

The reply buzzed back fast for someone with a sore throat. "Already photographed it for you. It depicts him mid-stride, phone to his ear, people staring."

Christopher remembered, suddenly, the mural on the median outside the school, painted with geese flying in a migratory V, and how Theodor had said phones were like that, everyone heading the same way. He showed Brennan the photo of Cooper walking down the street.

"Tomorrow," Christopher said, "I'm putting that picture as my wallpaper."

"Best first phone ever," said Brennan, and handed him the box to hold until morning.
